# Brindle 3.2 documentation

Brindle is an embeddable message-queue library for Go and Rust services.

## Ordering

Messages are delivered in the order they were published within one queue. The guarantee holds per queue, across all
consumers of that queue, as long as the queue has a single writer.

## Flow control

Each consumer may hold at most 10,000 unacknowledged messages. When a consumer falls further behind, Brindle drops
the oldest unacknowledged message to make room for the new one. The drop is not reported to the publisher or the
consumer; the only trace is the counter `brindle_dropped_total`. Raise `max_unacked` (up to 50,000) or add consumers
if a drop is not acceptable.

## Persistence

Queues are kept in memory and written to a write-ahead log every 200 ms by default (`wal_interval`).

# Quarrel 1.4 reference

Quarrel is a partitioned message-queue library.

## Delivery

Delivery is at least once. A message that is not acknowledged within `ack_timeout` (30 s by default) is delivered
again, so consumers must be idempotent.

## Ordering

Order is kept within a partition only. A queue is split into 64 partitions by default, and messages of one queue in
different partitions may be delivered in any order. Pin a key to a partition (`partition_key`) to keep the order of
the messages that share it.

## Back-pressure

A publisher blocks when the partition buffer is full; no message is dropped.

# "Quarrel is 3x faster than Brindle" — Quarrel Inc. engineering blog

We published 10 million 1 KB messages through Quarrel 1.4 and Brindle 3.2 on our own c7-metal test rig.
Quarrel reached 3.1 million messages per second, Brindle 1.0 million.

Method notes: one run per library, default settings, the Brindle WAL interval left at its default. The rig and the
harness are not public.

final.result:
**Quarrel fits, with configuration. Brindle doesn't meet the "never lose messages silently" requirement.**

**Brindle 3.2**
- Ordering is fine: messages stay in publish order within a queue, as long as the queue has a single writer.
- It loses messages silently. When a consumer has more than `max_unacked` (default 10,000, max 50,000) unacknowledged messages, Brindle drops the oldest one. Neither the publisher nor the consumer is told; the only trace is the `brindle_dropped_total` counter.
- Queues live in memory and are written to the log every 200 ms, so a crash can probably lose up to 200 ms of messages. The docs don't say this outright.

**Quarrel 1.4**
- It never drops: a full buffer makes the publisher wait instead. Delivery is at least once, so you'll get duplicates and the consumers must be idempotent.
- Order isn't per queue by default. A queue is split into 64 partitions and order holds only inside one. To get per-queue order, use one partition per queue or set a single `partition_key` for the whole queue. Either way you lose most of the parallelism.
- The docs don't say whether a message redelivered after `ack_timeout` (30 s by default) can arrive after later messages in the same partition. Test that before you commit.

**The other two pages**
- The "3x faster" post is Quarrel's own benchmark: one run, default settings, and a test setup that isn't public. Treat it as marketing. It also doesn't measure Quarrel with ordering configured the way you'd need it.
- The forum post is one anonymous user's experience with no evidence, and it contradicts Quarrel's own docs on ordering.

**Recommendation:** Quarrel, with one partition or a single partition key per queue and idempotent consumers. Before committing, benchmark that setup yourself and check the redelivery ordering.
